# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This follow-up is the strongest evidence in the set, and it answers several questions the earlier documents left open:
- The per-hour gain shrank but did not disappear.
- The counter arm failed in practice.
- The meetings pathway now has registered support, with the evidential limits set out below.

Its rebuttals of the re-analysis and of the meta-analysis's decay claim are mostly fair. Five problems need fixing:
1. The new log-hours measure is undefined, and as described it is hard to reconcile with the meeting data.
2. Two control offices changed their own practice mid-trial, which affects the decay estimate.
3. "Confirms" overstates what a mediation analysis on the same seven offices can show.
4. The Summary compares a nine-month figure and a 24-month figure on different hours measures.
5. Backlog and deadline data are still missing.

## Arithmetic check

- **Varden, timesheets:** 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098, so **+9.8%** ✓.
- **Varden, logs:** 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085, so **+8.5%** ✓.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 ✓.
- **Meeting time, difference-in-differences:** treated −3.5 hours, control −0.2 hours, so −3.3 hours. This matches the nine-month figure ✓.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 (−13.4%) ✓, and 0.968 / 0.866 = 1.118, so **+11.8%** ✓.
- **Decline from nine months:** 12.5% → 9.8% is about a 22% fall on the same measure, so "about a quarter" is generous but fair.
- **Counter costs:** 12% more staff giving 9% higher cost per contact implies labour is about 75% of costs. Plausible, but state the assumption.

## Major issues

**1. What do the system logs measure?**
The report describes logs as "active log-in time … working on cases." If that means time on the case system only, meetings are excluded. Then the numbers don't fit:
- Timesheet hours fell about 4.5 hours a week (12% of 37.9).
- Meeting time fell about 3.3 hours relative to control.
- So case-system time should have fallen only about 1–2 hours (about 3–5%), not 11%.

If instead logs record total logged-in time including meetings, they aren't a "stricter" measure of work, only a different one.

Either way, two claims need revisiting:
- **"Log data show slightly more work than timesheets."** Logs and timesheets measure different things, so comparing their percentage changes says little about unrecorded work.
- **The mediation design.** If meetings are inside the hours denominator, cutting them raises output per hour partly by construction. If they are outside it, the meetings pathway needs a different explanation, such as fewer interruptions.

Define the measure, give its baseline level in hours, and reconcile it with the meeting data.

**2. Two control offices adopted part of the treatment.**
The "meeting audit" in two of the seven control offices at month 15 is more than a side observation:
- **It shrinks the measured effect.** Those offices' output per hour rose about 4% from month 15. Averaged across seven controls, that lifts the control mean by roughly 1 point over the last nine months. Part of the 12.5% → 9.8% "fading" may therefore be controls improving, not treated offices declining.
- **Trial awareness may have triggered it.** Staff knew a trial was running, and the meetings finding had already been published.
- **The 4.1% itself is weak evidence.** It is a before–after change in two self-selected offices, possibly with regression to the mean if they audited because they were struggling.

Re-estimate the 24-month effect excluding those two offices, or excluding months 15–24 for them. Report it as a sensitivity analysis, and discuss contamination in the decay interpretation.

**3. The mediation result is weaker than "confirms."**
- **Same offices.** The registered test uses the same seven treated offices that generated the hypothesis. Registering at month 11 prevents choosing the model after seeing results, but it isn't independent replication.
- **Office-months inflate precision.** Mediators weren't randomised, and the effective sample is 14 clusters. If office-months were treated as independent, the CIs (28–66% for meetings) are too narrow. Say how clustering was handled. With this few clusters, use a cluster bootstrap.
- **The mediators interact.** Fewer meetings may themselves reduce fatigue, so the split between the two depends on model specification. Report the specification and its sensitivity.
- **Wording.** The Limitations section correctly notes the no-confounding assumption. The Summary should match: "a registered mediation analysis is consistent with meetings accounting for about half of the gain," not "confirms."

**4. The headline decline mixes measures.**
The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data." The 12.5% is a timesheet figure. The like-for-like comparison is **12.5% → 9.8%**, and the move to logs is a separate change. The two intervals (6.9–18.4 vs 4.6–15.2) also overlap substantially. Test the change formally before calling it a decline.

**5. Backlog and deadlines are still unreported.**
The nine-month report flagged "whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines" as the key long-run risk. At 24 months, output per FTE is drifting down (−2.1% → −3.4%). Backlog size, time to decision and the share of cases past deadline are in the case-management system and should be in Table 1.

## Halden section

- **Selection is now three layers deep.** Organisations volunteered, completed the pilot and chose to continue (as the authors note). In addition, only 14 of the 23 organisations asked agreed to provide data.
- **"Upper bound" isn't guaranteed.** A 24-month before–after comparison with no control is exposed to two years of general trends: economic conditions, new tools, staff turnover. These could push the estimate in either direction, so the figure is uncontrolled, not bounded.
- **Check the 40.3-hour baseline.** It is identical to the 27-organisation time-tracking baseline in the re-analysis. Confirm that it is these 11 organisations' own baseline, and that all 11 have time-tracking data. Only 17 Halden organisations had both records and time tracking.
- **The marketing agency doesn't fit the dichotomy.** The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations." A marketing agency citing client deadlines is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding. It is the first reversion outside the coverage-bound sectors and should be reported as such.
- **Reverting organisations should be in the follow-up estimate.** Their output indices were 88–91 at reversion. An intention-to-treat figure covering all 14 would be more informative than the continuers-only 11.8%.

## Smaller points

- **Counter arm.** Report the full months 10–12 difference-in-differences results (output per FTE, per hour, abandonment), not only waiting times. Earlier I noted that abandonment didn't explain the size of the output fall, and that question is still open.
- **Sick days (−27%).** This still needs expressing per scheduled day. Resignations need CIs.
- **Meeting baseline.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. The 7.4- and 7.2-hour baselines must have come from historical calendars. Say so; this also resolves the "cut most" problem I raised on the nine-month report.
- **Rebuttal of the energy extrapolation.** It is fair, though note that the extrapolation actually crossed zero at about month 9, and it was based on Halden employees, not Varden staff.
- **Response to the meta-analysis.** This is sound and confirms the concern I raised: all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours.
- **Author overlap.** The authors are adjudicating claims about their own earlier work, and Okafor is Halden's lead author. A competing-interests statement would help.

## Updated picture

| | Discretionary work | Coverage-bound work |
|---|---|---|
| Varden, 9 months | +12.5% per hour; output per worker −2.1% | +6.7% per hour; output per worker −11.4%; longer waits |
| Varden, 24 months | +9.8% (timesheets) / +8.5% (logs) per hour; output per worker −3.4% | Arm ended at month 12; restoring service would cost about +9% per contact |
| Halden continuers, 24 months (uncontrolled) | +11.8% per actual hour | 2 of 3 reversions; output 88–91 at reversion |
| Meta-analysis (controlled discretionary) | +9.6% per hour; output per worker −2.7% | output per worker −8.9% |

Taken together:
- **Discretionary work:** A real per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at two years, with some fading, possibly overstated by control-office contamination. Output per worker is slightly below what it would otherwise have been, by about 2–4%.
- **Coverage-bound work:** With headcount fixed, reduced hours worsened service enough that the county ended the arm.
- **Mechanism:** Removing low-value meeting time is the leading candidate. Whether it requires the hours cut to happen is untested; that would need an arm that reorganises without reducing hours.

I can draft a referee report or a closing synthesis of all five documents.
